title: A sense of self: how your body knows its own touch, voice and likes

summary.text: Why can't you tickle yourself? When you stroke your own foot, it hardly tickles. When someone else does the same, you laugh. Your brain knows which touches you are making, a moment before they land. In this unit you test that, hear your own voice the way others hear it, and find out which of your likes have changed since you were small.
summary.art: A girl of 7 sitting on a mat, stroking the sole of her own bare foot with a feather and looking puzzled, while a family member holds another feather and smiles.

intro.text: Take off one sock. Stroke the bottom of your foot gently with your own finger, five times. Now ask someone at home to do the same, the same way. Which one made you want to laugh? Keep your answer in mind. Soon you will test it properly.
intro.art: A bare child's foot with a finger stroking the sole, and beside it a second picture of a grown-up's hand doing the same.

outcomes: By the end I can say what a sense of self is: knowing that this body, these likes and these feelings are mine.
By the end I can explain why my own touch tickles less than someone else's touch.
By the end I can do a fair test with the same tool, the same spot and the same number of strokes, and count the results.
By the end I can explain why my voice sounds different on a recording.
By the end I can give an example of a like that has changed since I was small.
By the end I can say how other living beings, such as a plant or a cricket, tell their own from another's.

terms.meaning: Your self is you: your body, your thoughts, your likes and your feelings.
terms.example: When you say 'I am hungry', the 'I' is your self.
terms.art: A girl pointing at her own chest with a smile.

terms.meaning: A sense of self is knowing that you are you, and that your body is yours.
terms.example: You know that the hand at the end of your arm is your hand, without looking.
terms.art: A child with eyes closed touching their own nose with one finger.

terms.meaning: To predict is to know or guess what will happen before it happens.
terms.example: When you lift your foot to step, your brain predicts the floor will push back.
terms.art: A girl about to catch a ball, her hands already in the right place.

terms.meaning: A tickle is a light touch that makes you squirm or laugh.
terms.example: A feather stroked on the bottom of your foot can tickle.
terms.art: A feather stroking a foot, with small laugh lines in the air.

terms.meaning: To vibrate is to shake back and forth very fast. Sound is made by things that vibrate.
terms.example: Put your fingers on your throat and hum. You can feel it vibrate.
terms.art: Two fingers on a child's throat while she hums, with small wavy lines.

terms.meaning: A feeling is what happens inside you when you are happy, scared, angry, sad or excited. Another word for it is emotion.
terms.example: Before a race you might feel excited and a little scared at the same time.
terms.art: A boy at a school race start line, with a nervous smile.

terms.meaning: A like is something you enjoy and choose when you can. A dislike is something you would rather not have.
terms.example: You might like mango and dislike bitter gourd.
terms.art: A plate with a slice of mango and a piece of bitter gourd, a girl pointing happily at the mango.

explanations.context: This card is about what a sense of self means.
explanations.definition: A sense of self is knowing that you are you: that this body is yours, and these likes, feelings and thoughts are yours.
explanations.description: You do not have to think about it. You know your hand is yours without looking, and you know what you like and how you feel inside. Babies start to know some of this very early. Newborn babies turn their head more when someone else touches their cheek than when their own hand touches it.
examples: You can touch your nose with your eyes shut, because you know where your body is.
You know a feeling is yours, even if no one else can see it.
Most children know themselves in a mirror by about 2 years old.
explanations.art: A girl with her eyes shut, touching her nose, with a small mirror on the table beside her.

explanations.context: This card explains the tickle test, where you stroked your own foot and then someone else stroked it.
explanations.definition: When you move, your brain predicts the touch your movement will make, and turns that feeling down.
explanations.description: When you move your hand, your brain sends a message to the muscles and keeps a copy. From the copy, your brain predicts what you will feel. When the touch arrives just as predicted, your brain turns the feeling down. Someone else's touch cannot be predicted so well, so it feels stronger and it tickles.
examples: Your own finger on your foot hardly tickles.
Someone else's finger, moving the same way, tickles a lot.
Touches that are always there fade too. You do not notice your clothes on your skin until you think about them.
explanations.art: A simple drawing: a child's brain with an arrow to the hand, and a dotted arrow 'copy' that meets the arrow coming back from the foot.

explanations.concept: Why your voice sounds strange on a recording
explanations.context: This card explains the recording activity, where you heard your own voice on a phone.
explanations.definition: You hear your own voice through the air and through the bones of your head. Other people hear it only through the air.
explanations.description: When you talk, your throat vibrates. The sound goes through the air into everyone's ears, and into yours. The vibration also travels through the bones of your head to your inner ear, and bones carry low sounds well. So your voice sounds deeper to you. A phone records only the sound in the air, which is what everyone else hears.
examples: Most people say 'That's not me!' the first time they hear a recording of themselves.
Your family says the recording sounds just like you.
Hum with your ears blocked by your fingers, and the hum gets louder inside your head.
explanations.art: A girl talking, with wavy lines going out through the air to her mother's ear, and other wavy lines going through her own head to her ear.

explanations.concept: Your likes and feelings are yours, and they change
explanations.context: This card is about likes and feelings, and the 'then and now' activity, where you asked what you liked when you were small.
explanations.description: Only you feel your feelings from the inside. Other people see clues, such as your face or your voice, and they guess. Your likes are yours too, but many of them change as you grow. Newborn babies already like sweet tastes and pull a face at bitter ones. Many other likes come from what you meet and try. Scientists are still finding out which likes we are born with and which we learn.
examples: You might have hated a food at 3 and like it now.
A grown-up may still love the songs they liked as a child.
You can feel scared inside while your face looks calm.

perspectives.explanation: Some likes are there from birth, such as liking sweet tastes. Others are learnt from trying things many times.
Even the likes we are born with change a lot with what our family eats and does, so most likes are learnt.

explanations.art: Two drawings side by side: a toddler pushing away a plate of green beans, and the same girl at 7 eating them happily.

explanations.concept: Other beings know their own from another's
explanations.context: This card is about whether other living beings, not only humans, tell themselves apart from others.
explanations.description: Humans are not the only beings who tell their own from another's. Pollen is the fine dust that flowers make. Many flowers know their own pollen and stop it from making seeds. Roots of some grasses grow differently near their own roots than near roots of another plant. A male cricket sings very loudly, and his hearing turns down while he sings, so his own song does not deafen him. Your brain does something like this when you tickle yourself. Plants and crickets sense, decide and know their own. Some scientists call this an automatic response and say a real sense of self needs a brain like ours.
examples: A flower keeps their own pollen from making seeds, and lets in pollen from another plant.
A singing cricket turns down his own hearing while he sings.
Newborn human babies turn their head more to someone else's touch than to their own.

perspectives.who: Many biologists who study plants and insects
perspectives.explanation: A flower that rejects their own pollen and a cricket that quiets his own song are telling 'me' from 'not me'. That is a sense of self, in their own way.
These are chemical and nerve responses. A sense of self, they say, means knowing 'this is me', and that needs a brain.

explanations.art: A flower with pollen grains, a green cricket singing on a leaf, and a newborn baby turning to a finger on their cheek.

agreed.text: Your own touch feels weaker than the same touch from someone else. This is why most people cannot tickle themselves.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have tested people with tickling machines since 1971. In these tests people rated their own touch as less ticklish.

agreed.text: Your voice sounds different to you than to others, because you also hear it through the bones of your head.
agreed.evidence: When people hear their voice with their ears blocked, it sounds deeper. A recording picks up only the sound in the air, so it sounds higher to the person who spoke.

agreed.text: A sense of self starts very early. Newborn babies react differently to their own touch and someone else's.
agreed.evidence: In 1997 Philippe Rochat and Susan Hespos watched newborn babies. The babies turned to a finger on their cheek more often than to their own hand.

challenging.claim: You cannot tickle yourself only because you know when the touch is coming.
challenging.for: When you tickle yourself you do know when and where the touch will be.
challenging.against: In Sarah-Jayne Blakemore's tests, people moved a robot that touched their own hand. They knew exactly when the touch would come. When the robot added a tiny delay, the touch tickled more. So knowing is not enough. The brain has to predict the touch exactly.
challenging.context: This card is about why your own touch tickles less.

challenging.claim: Only beings with big brains can tell themselves apart from others.
challenging.for: Knowing 'this is me' in a mirror has been seen mostly in animals with big brains, such as apes, elephants and dolphins.
challenging.against: Flowers reject their own pollen, roots treat their own roots differently, and crickets quiet their own song. Telling self from other is found all through life.
challenging.context: This card is about who has a sense of self.

challenging.claim: Your likes are fixed. You are born liking some things and not others.
challenging.for: Newborn babies already like sweet tastes and dislike bitter ones.
challenging.against: Many children come to like a food after tasting it again and again. Most people's likes in food, music and games change as they grow.
challenging.context: This card is about whether likes can change.

big_questions.q: Your voice sounds one way to you and another way to everyone else. Which one is your real voice?
big_questions.hint: Your family hears your voice through the air. You hear it through the air and through the bones of your head together. Is that one voice heard in two ways, or two different voices?

big_questions.q: Your brain turns down the feeling of your own touch. What else might your brain be turning down without telling you?
big_questions.hint: Think of your clothes on your skin, or your tongue in your mouth. Do you feel them right now?

big_questions.q: If your likes keep changing, which of them are really you?
big_questions.hint: Think of a like you had at 3 that has gone, and one you still have.

big_questions.q: A flower knows their own pollen. Does that flower have a sense of self?
big_questions.hint: What would the flower have to do for you to say yes? What would make you say no?

big_questions.q: Only you feel your feelings from the inside. Can anyone else ever know exactly how you feel?
big_questions.hint: They can see your face and hear your words. Is that the same as feeling it?

story.title: Kavya's Two Voices
story.note: A made-up story. It is true that we hear our own voice through the bones of the head as well as the air, and that people's own touch tickles them less.
text: Kavya lived on the fifth floor of a building in Kochi. She was seven. She lived with her Appa, her baby cousin Anu who came to stay on weekends, and her grandmother, Ammachi. Ammachi had been a nurse for thirty years.
One rainy Saturday, Appa was making a video on his phone for Kavya's aunt in Chennai. "Say hello to Chithi," he said, and pointed the phone at Kavya.
"Hello, Chithi! It is raining so much here!" said Kavya.
Appa played the video back. Kavya's mouth fell open. "That is not me," she said. "That girl has a squeaky voice. My voice is not like that."
"That is exactly your voice," said Appa, laughing. "It sounds just like you."
Kavya frowned. "Ammachi, is the phone broken?"
Ammachi put down the beans she was cutting. "The phone is fine," she said. "Put your fingers on your throat and hum."
Kavya hummed. Her fingers buzzed. "It is shaking!"

"Your throat vibrates when you talk," said Ammachi. "The sound goes out through the air to Appa's ears. But it also goes through the bones of your head, straight into your own ears. Bones carry the deep part of a sound very well. So you hear yourself deeper than everyone else does. The phone hears only the air, like Appa."
"So there are two Kavya voices?" asked Kavya.
"There is one voice," said Ammachi. "You hear it from the inside, and we hear it from the outside."
Kavya thought about this for a long time. Then Anu, who was nearly one, crawled over and grabbed her toe. Kavya squealed and pulled her foot away.
"You are so ticklish," said Appa. He reached for her foot.
"No! Wait," said Kavya. She stroked her own foot with her finger. Nothing. She did it again, harder. Still nothing. "Look, Appa. When I do it, it does not tickle at all."
"That is because you know it is coming," said Appa.
"Is that true, Ammachi?" asked Kavya.
Ammachi smiled. "Let us test it, instead of guessing. Fetch the peacock feather from the shelf, and a pencil and paper."
They drew four faces on the paper. A straight face meant 0, not ticklish. A small smile meant 1. A big smile meant 2. A laughing face meant 3, very ticklish.

First Kavya stroked her own foot with the feather, five slow strokes, with her eyes shut. Then she opened them and pointed at the straight face. Then Ammachi stroked the same spot with the same feather, five slow strokes. Kavya kicked and laughed. She pointed at the laughing face.
"Now Appa," said Kavya. Appa took off his socks, looking worried. He stroked his own foot. Zero. Kavya stroked it. Appa giggled so much that Anu laughed too. Three.
They tested each person twice. Every time, the person's own touch scored lower than someone else's touch.

"Appa, you said it is because you know it is coming," said Kavya. "But my eyes were shut when Ammachi did it, and I still knew she was going to stroke me. I knew where. I knew it was coming. And it still tickled."
Appa scratched his head. "Then why does the feather not tickle when you do it yourself?"

Ammachi said, "When you move your hand, your brain sends a message to your muscles. It keeps a copy too. From the copy it works out exactly what you will feel, at exactly the right moment. When the touch arrives just as expected, the brain turns it down. My hand is not your hand. Your brain cannot work out my strokes so exactly."
"So my brain knows which touches are mine," said Kavya slowly. "And it knows which voice is mine, from the inside."
That evening Kavya showed Appa one more thing. She hummed with her fingers in her ears. "Try it," she said. Appa hummed with his fingers in his ears. His eyes went wide. "It is so loud inside!"
"That is your bone voice," said Kavya. "Ammachi taught me. Now I am teaching you."
Anu crawled over again and grabbed Appa's toe. Appa squealed. Everybody laughed, and nobody could stop for a long time.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kavya first thinks the phone has got her voice wrong, and Appa thinks you can't tickle yourself only because you know the touch is coming. A fair test with a feather shows that knowing is not enough. Kavya ends up seeing that her body knows its own voice and its own touch from the inside.
ask: Why did Kavya think the phone was broken?
What did they keep the same each time in the feather test?
What does Ammachi say the brain keeps when you move your hand?
What did Kavya teach Appa at the end?
art: A Kochi flat on a rainy day, a father holding up a phone to film his daughter while a grandmother cuts beans at the table.
A girl with her eyes shut stroking her own foot with a peacock feather, a paper with four faces on the floor beside her.
A father laughing hard while his daughter strokes his foot with a feather, and a baby laughing on the floor.
A father and daughter humming with their fingers in their ears, eyes wide.

experiments.title: The Tickle Test: does your own touch tickle less?
experiments.context: In this experiment you stroke the bottom of your own foot with a feather and give it a tickle score. Then someone else strokes it in exactly the same way, and you score it again. You test everyone at home who wants to play, and count the results.
experiments.question: Does your own stroke on your foot tickle less, more, or the same as someone else's stroke done the same way?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will your own stroke tickle less, more or the same as someone else's? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same feather, the same spot on the foot, and the same five slow strokes every time. Keep your eyes shut for the strokes, then open them to point to a face. Each person gets two tries of each kind, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a feather, or a soft paintbrush, or a cotton bud, or a strip of newspaper rolled into a thin stick
a paper with four faces drawn on it: straight face 0, small smile 1, big smile 2, laughing face 3
at least one other person at home who agrees to play

schedule.what: Guess, then test everyone twice with their own stroke and twice with someone else's stroke. Count the results.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then count how many people had a lower score for their own stroke.

setup.art: A paper with four faces in a row, numbered 0 to 3, from a straight face to a laughing face, and a feather beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the four tickle faces and find a feather.

setup.art: A girl sitting on a mat with her eyes shut, stroking the sole of her own bare foot with a feather.
setup.caption: 2. Stroke your own foot five times, eyes shut. Open them and point to a face.

setup.art: A parent stroking the sole of the same girl's foot with the same feather, the girl laughing with eyes shut.
setup.caption: 3. Someone else strokes the same spot five times. Point to a face.

setup.art: A results table on paper with names down the side and numbers 0 to 3 in the boxes.
setup.caption: 4. Write the scores and count.

flow.do: Ask the question and wait for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the paper.
flow.say: We are going to test tickles. Will your own stroke tickle less, more or the same as mine? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will your own stroke tickle less, more or the same? Why?

good: Less, because I know when it is coming.
The same, because a feather is a feather.
More, because I can press harder.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine if it has a reason. Do not say what will happen. Tickle only people who say yes, and stop the moment anyone says stop.

flow.do: 1. Draw the four faces: straight face 0, small smile 1, big smile 2, laughing face 3. 2. Make the results table.
flow.say: These faces are our tickle scores. Zero means not ticklish at all. Three means very ticklish.
flow.kid: Draw four faces. Zero is a straight face. Three is a laughing face.

flow.do: Agree the fair rules together and say them out loud: same feather, same spot, five slow strokes, eyes shut.
flow.say: What must we keep the same each time, so the test is fair?
flow.kid: Keep it fair. Use the same feather and the same spot. Do five slow strokes, with your eyes shut.

ask.q: Why must the strokes be the same?
good: So only who is stroking changes.
If one stroke is harder, that is not fair.

flow.do: 1. The child strokes the middle of their own sole five times with eyes shut, then opens them and points to a face. 2. The child shuts their eyes again. You stroke the same spot five times at the same speed, and the child opens their eyes and points to a face. 3. Repeat both once more. 4. Write every score.
flow.say: First your own stroke, eyes shut. Open them and point to a face. Now my stroke, the same way. Point to a face again.
flow.kid: Stroke your own foot five times, eyes shut. Open them and point to a face. Now let someone else do it. Point again.
flow.parent: Try to copy the child's strokes: same pressure, same speed. If the sole is not ticklish for anyone, use the side of the foot instead.

flow.do: Swap. Test every other person at home who agrees, the same way, two tries each.
flow.say: Now let's test someone else at home who wants to play. Who will stroke their own foot first?
flow.kid: Now test someone else at home. You do the stroking for them.

flow.do: Count together. How many people had a lower score for their own stroke? How many the same? How many higher?
flow.say: Look at the table. What did you notice? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Count. For how many people did their own stroke tickle less? Was your guess right?

good: My own stroke got 0 or 1, and the other person's got 3.

flow.parent: Most people score their own stroke lower, often 0 or 1. A few find their own stroke a little tickly too, but it is usually still lower. If your result is different, write it down as it is. Only after the child has said what they saw, read the card on why you can't tickle yourself.
flow.think: Your eyes were shut both times, and you knew the stroke was coming. So why was there a difference?

check.q: You stroke your own foot five times and score 0. Someone else strokes it the same way, and you score 3. What does this show?
options: Your own stroke tickles less than someone else's
The other person pressed harder, so it is not fair
check.why: If the strokes were the same, the only change was who made them. Your brain predicted your own stroke and turned the feeling down.

experiments.title: The Glove Hand: can your brain take a glove for your hand?
experiments.context: In this experiment you hide your real hand and look at a kitchen glove filled with water instead. Someone strokes the glove and your hidden hand at the same moment. You find out whether the glove starts to feel like your own hand.
experiments.question: If you watch a glove being stroked while your hidden hand is stroked at the same time, does the glove start to feel like your hand?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the glove start to feel like part of you, or will it always feel like just a glove? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Do it twice. In the first try, stroke the glove and the real hand at exactly the same moment. In the second try, stroke them at different moments. Only the timing changes.
results_table: Same moment: did the glove feel like my hand? (yes, a bit, no)
Different moments: did the glove feel like my hand? (yes, a bit, no)

materials.item: a rubber kitchen glove or dishwashing glove, filled with water and tied, or stuffed with cloth
a big book, a tray or a cereal box to stand up as a wall
two soft paintbrushes, or two cotton buds

schedule.what: Set up the glove and the book that hides the hand. Then do the same-moment strokes and the different-moment strokes, and ask each person what they felt.

experiments.record: Write yes, a bit or no for each try. Draw the set-up.

setup.art: A table with a standing book. A child's real left hand lies behind the book, out of sight. A water-filled glove lies in front of the child, where the hand would be.
setup.caption: 1. Hide the real hand behind a book. Put the glove where you can see it.

setup.art: A towel draped from the child's shoulder to the glove's wrist, so the glove looks joined to the arm.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the gap with a towel.

setup.art: A grown-up holding two paintbrushes, stroking one finger of the glove and the same finger of the hidden hand.
setup.caption: 3. Stroke the same finger on both, at the same moment.

flow.do: Fill the glove with water over a sink and tie the top tightly. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will hide your hand and stroke a glove. Will the glove feel like your hand? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will the glove feel like your hand? Why?

flow.do: 1. The child sits with both arms on the table. 2. Stand a book up to hide their left hand. 3. Put the glove 15 cm from the hidden hand, in line with the arm. 4. Drape a towel from the child's shoulder to the glove.
flow.say: Keep your hidden hand very still. Look only at the glove.
flow.kid: Keep your hidden hand still. Look at the glove.

flow.do: Stroke the same finger of the glove and of the hidden hand at exactly the same moment, slowly, for about two minutes.
flow.say: Keep watching the glove. Tell me if anything changes.
flow.kid: Watch the glove. Say if it starts to feel like your hand.

flow.do: First take the towel off and let the child shake their hands out for a minute. Then put the towel back. Now stroke the glove and the hand at different moments: first the glove, then the hand, for two minutes.
flow.say: This time I will stroke them at different moments. Does it feel the same?
flow.kid: Now the strokes come at different times. Is it different?

flow.do: Ask what they felt in each try, and write it down. If there is time, swap and try it on another person.
flow.say: Did the glove ever feel like your hand? In which try?
flow.kid: Did the glove feel like your hand? When?
flow.parent: Scientists found this works for many people, but not for everyone. If it does not work, that is a real result too. Write it down. It is not a failure.
flow.think: Your brain decided which hand was yours by putting seeing and feeling together. What happens when they don't match?

activities.title: That's Not Me! Hear your voice the way others hear it
activities.context: In this activity you record your voice on a phone and listen to it. Then you ask your family whether it sounds like you.

materials.item: a phone that can record sound

schedule.what: Record a sentence, listen, ask the family, then hum with fingers in your ears.

activities.record: Write how many people said the recording sounds like you, and how many said it doesn't.

setup.art: A girl speaking into a phone held by a parent.
setup.caption: 1. Record yourself saying one sentence.

setup.art: A girl listening to the phone with a surprised face, while a family member nods.
setup.caption: 2. Listen. Ask your family: is that me?

setup.art: A girl humming with her fingers in her ears.
setup.caption: 3. Hum with your fingers in your ears.

flow.do: Record the child saying one sentence, for example their name and their favourite food.
flow.say: Say your name and your favourite food. I will record it.
flow.kid: Say your name and your favourite food into the phone.

flow.do: Play it back. Ask the child, then ask everyone else at home.
flow.say: Does that sound like you? Now let's ask everyone else.
flow.kid: Listen. Does it sound like you? Ask your family too.
flow.parent: Most children say it does not sound like them, while the family says it does. Both are right.

flow.do: The child puts two fingers on their throat and hums, then hums with fingers gently in their ears.
flow.say: Hum with your fingers on your throat. Now hum with your fingers in your ears. What changed?
flow.kid: Hum. Feel your throat shake. Now hum with fingers in your ears. Is it louder?

flow.do: Count the family's answers together.
flow.say: How many people said the recording sounds just like you?
flow.kid: Count. How many said it sounds like you?
flow.think: Which is your real voice, the one you hear or the one we hear?

activities.title: Then and Now: what did I like when I was three?
activities.context: In this activity you ask a grown-up what you liked when you were three years old. Then you say what you like now, and see which likes have changed.

materials.item: a sheet of paper folded in half, with 'When I was 3' on one side and 'Now' on the other

schedule.what: Interview a grown-up about your likes at 3, then fill in your likes now and compare.

activities.record: The folded paper with five likes on each side, and a tick next to each like that stayed the same.

setup.art: A paper folded in half, the left side headed 'When I was 3', the right side 'Now', with five rows each: food, toy, song, colour, game.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a paper and write five rows.

setup.art: A girl asking a grown-up questions while writing on the folded paper.
setup.caption: 2. Ask a grown-up what you liked at 3.

flow.do: Fold the paper. A parent writes the five row words on each side: food, toy, song, colour, game.
flow.say: We will find out what you liked when you were three. Do you remember?
flow.kid: Help write the five rows: food, toy, song, colour, game.

flow.do: The child asks a grown-up who knew them then, row by row, what they liked at 3. The child draws the answers on the left, or the grown-up writes them.
flow.say: Ask me, or another grown-up who knew you then: what was my favourite food when I was three?
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up: what did I like at 3? Draw or write it.

flow.do: The child fills in the right side with what they like now.
flow.say: Now fill in what you like today.
flow.kid: Now write what you like today.

flow.do: Count how many likes stayed the same and how many changed.
flow.say: How many likes are the same? How many changed? Why do you think they changed?
flow.kid: Count the same ones. Count the changed ones. Why did they change?

good: I grew bigger and can do new things.

flow.think: If most of your likes changed, are you still the same you?

activities.title: Mirror Me, Photo Me: which one do you like better?
activities.context: In this activity you look at yourself in a mirror and in a photo. A mirror shows you the other way round from a photo. Other people see you the way a photo does.

schedule.what: Put a sticker on one cheek, look in the mirror, take a photo, and compare the two.

activities.record: Draw yourself as the mirror shows you and as the photo shows you. Mark which cheek has the sticker.

setup.art: A girl with a small sticker on her right cheek looking into a mirror, the sticker on the right side of the reflection.
setup.caption: 1. Put a sticker on one cheek. Look in the mirror.

setup.art: A phone screen showing a photo of the same girl, with the sticker on the left side of the picture.
setup.caption: 2. Take a photo. Where is the sticker now?

flow.do: Put a sticker on the child's right cheek. The child looks in the mirror and lifts their right hand.
flow.say: Lift your right hand. Which hand does the you in the mirror lift? Where is the sticker in the mirror?
flow.kid: Lift your right hand. Look at yourself in the mirror. Which hand did the mirror you lift?

flow.do: Someone else takes a photo of the child facing the camera, using the back camera, and shows it. A selfie view on a phone is often flipped like a mirror.
flow.say: Now look at the photo. Is the sticker on the same side as in the mirror?
flow.kid: Look at the photo. Where is the sticker?

flow.do: Ask which picture looks more like them, then ask the family the same question.
flow.say: Which one looks more like you, the mirror or the photo? Let's ask everyone.
flow.kid: Which one looks like you? Ask your family too.
flow.parent: In a study in 1977, many people liked their mirror face better, while their friends liked the photo better. The researchers thought each person liked the face they were used to seeing.
flow.think: You see the mirror you every day. Your friends see the photo you. Which is the real you?

activities.title: Find Your Own Touch: what is your brain turning down right now?
activities.context: In this activity you notice touches your brain usually turns down: your clothes, your tongue, your own breath.

schedule.what: Sit still and notice four touches you did not feel a minute ago.

activities.record: Draw yourself and mark the four places where you found a touch.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed, small dots on the shoulders, tongue and feet.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still and close your eyes.

setup.art: A child pointing to a sock on their foot with a surprised face.
setup.caption: 2. Notice a touch you did not feel before.

flow.do: The child sits still with eyes closed.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Can you feel your shirt on your shoulders? Were you feeling it a minute ago?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Feel your shirt on your shoulders.

flow.do: Name three more touches, one by one. First the floor under the feet. Then the tongue in the mouth. Then the breath under the nose.
flow.say: Now feel your feet on the floor. Now feel your tongue in your mouth. Now the air under your nose.
flow.kid: Feel your feet. Feel your tongue. Feel your breath.

flow.do: Talk about why these touches were not noticed before.
flow.say: Why didn't you notice these before?
flow.kid: Why didn't you feel them before?

good: My brain turns down touches that are always there.
Because they are my own and they don't change.

games.title: Me or Not Me?
games.context: This is a talking game about what counts as part of you. Each card names something, like your shadow or a hair that fell out. Players put it in the Me pile, the Not me pile or the Not sure pile, and say why.

printables.title: 12 cards to cut out, with a fact on the back

items.b: You know your hand is yours without looking. Your brain keeps track of where it is.

items.f: A hair that fell out yesterday
items.b: A fallen hair is made of the same material as the hair on your head, but it no longer grows.
Your shadow is a patch where your body blocks the light. It moves when you move.

items.f: Your voice on a phone recording
items.b: Your family hears this voice. You hear a deeper one, through the bones of your head.
In a mirror, your sides look swapped compared with a photo. Other people see you the way a photo does.

items.f: A milk tooth that fell out
items.b: A milk tooth grew in your mouth for years. Now a new tooth grows in its place.

items.f: The breath you just breathed out
items.b: Your body added water vapour and carbon dioxide to this air. Plants take in carbon dioxide.
Your family chose your name. It was not part of you when you were born.
Likes are yours, but many of them change as you grow.
Only you feel it from the inside. Others can only see clues.
You made it with your hand and your ideas. It is outside your body now.

items.f: The food you ate at lunch
items.b: Food you eat is broken down and becomes part of your body.

rules: Make three piles on the floor: Me, Not me and Not sure. Write each name on a scrap of paper.
Mix the cards and stack them with the name side up and the fact side down.
Take turns. Pick the top card, read it aloud and put it on a pile. A grown-up reads it if you cannot yet.
Say one reason. Anyone who disagrees can say why.
Turn the card over and read the fact. You can move the card if you change your mind.
There is no winner and no single right answer. The game ends when all 12 cards are placed. Count the cards on each pile.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and make three piles.
flow.say: Some things are clearly you, some clearly not, and some are hard to decide. Let's sort them.
flow.kid: Make three piles: Me, Not me and Not sure.

flow.do: Play the game, taking turns. Ask for a reason each time.
flow.say: Why did you put your shadow there?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Put it on a pile. Say why.

ask.q: Why is it on that pile?
good: My hand is me, because I can feel it.
I put my shadow on Not sure, because it moves with me but nobody can touch it.

flow.do: Count the piles and talk about the Not sure cards.
flow.say: Which card was the hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Count each pile. Which card was hardest?
flow.think: Did anyone in your family put a card on a different pile from you?

setup.art: Twelve small cards in a face-down pile, and three paper labels on the floor: Me, Not me, Not sure.
setup.caption: 1. Make three piles and mix the cards.

setup.art: A girl putting a card that says 'Your shadow' on the Not sure pile, while a parent listens.
setup.caption: 2. Pick a card, put it on a pile, and say why.

games.title: Who Likes What? A guessing game
games.context: This is a guessing game about likes. Each player secretly writes their favourites. The others guess them. You find out how well your family knows your likes, and how well you know theirs.

printables.title: A likes sheet with 6 lines: copy it once for each player

rules: Each player fills in their likes sheet in secret, and folds it.
Pick one player to start. Everyone else guesses that player's favourite food, one at a time. With 2 players, the other player guesses.
The player opens their sheet and reads the answer. Each right guess gets one point for the guesser. A guess is right if it matches the sheet.
Do the same for colour, sound, smell and time of day.
Take turns until every player has had their sheet read.
The player with the most points wins. If two players have the same number, they both win.

flow.do: Give each player a likes sheet. Everyone fills it in secretly.
flow.say: Write your favourites. Don't show anyone.
flow.kid: Write your favourites in secret.

flow.do: Play, guessing each player's likes in turn. Keep a tally of right guesses.
flow.say: What do you think my favourite smell is?
flow.kid: Guess. What does the other person like best?

flow.do: Talk about the results.
flow.say: Who guessed your likes best? Were any of your likes a surprise to the others?
flow.kid: Who knows your likes best? Which like surprised them?
flow.think: Do you know all of your own likes? Did you have to think hard about any of them?

setup.art: Four folded paper sheets on a mat, each with a name on the outside.
setup.caption: 1. Fill in your likes in secret and fold the sheet.

setup.art: A family sitting in a circle, one person opening her sheet and reading it while the others wait.
setup.caption: 2. Guess, then open the sheet and read the answer.

projects.title: My Me Book: five pages, one a day
projects.context: In this project you make a small book about yourself, one page each day: your body, your voice, your likes, your feelings, and what others see in you.

materials.item: five sheets of paper, folded and stapled or tied with thread into a book

schedule.what: Page 1, My body: draw round your hand and write three things your body can do.
Page 2, My voice: write what your recorded voice sounded like (from That's Not Me!), and what your family said.
Page 3, My likes: draw three likes now and one like that changed (from Then and Now).
Page 4, My feelings: draw a face for how you felt this morning, at lunch and now.
Page 5, What others see: ask two people to say one thing they know about you, and write it. Then read the whole book aloud to someone.

setup.art: Five sheets of paper folded in half and tied with a thread into a small book, with 'Me' written on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Make a five-page book.

setup.art: An open page with a child's hand traced in pencil and three short lines written beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Fill one page each day.

flow.do: Day 1. A parent folds the five sheets into a book. The child draws round their hand and writes three things their body can do, or says them for a parent to write.
flow.say: This is your Me book. Today's page is your body. What can your body do?
flow.kid: Draw round your hand. Write three things your body can do.

flow.do: Day 2. The child fills in the voice page, using what they found in the That's Not Me! activity.
flow.say: What did your voice sound like on the phone? What did the family say?
flow.kid: Write about your voice on the phone.

flow.do: Day 3. The child fills in the likes page, using their Then and Now paper.
flow.say: Which three things do you like now? Which like has changed since you were small?
flow.kid: Draw three likes you have now and one that changed.

flow.do: Day 4. The child fills in the feelings page with three faces: morning, lunch and now.
flow.say: How did you feel this morning? At lunch? Now?
flow.kid: Draw three faces. Morning, lunch and now.

flow.do: Day 5. The child asks two people one thing they know about them, and writes it or draws it.
flow.say: Ask two people: what is one thing you know about me?
flow.kid: Ask two people. What do they know about you?
flow.think: Did they say something you didn't know about yourself?

flow.do: Read the whole book together.
flow.say: Read your Me book to us. Which page was the hardest to make?
flow.kid: Read your book out loud. Which page was hardest?

challenges.title: Build a Self-Tickle Machine
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Scientists found that if a machine adds a tiny delay, or moves the touch in a different direction from your hand, your own touch tickles more. Can you build a machine at home that makes your own touch tickle?
challenges.problem: Make something that moves a feather on your foot when you move your hand, but not in the same direction or at the same moment.
constraints: Use only things from home, such as string, a pencil, a ruler, tape and a feather.
You must be the only one moving it.
Test it fairly: same spot, five strokes, eyes shut.
materials: a feather or a paper strip
general: Tape the feather to the end of a ruler and hold the other end, so your hand is far from the feather. Your brain may still predict this stroke, so it may not tickle more. Test it and see.
Loop a string over the back of a chair, tie the feather to one end, and pull the other end down, so the feather moves up.
creative: Make the string loose, so the feather moves a moment after your hand.
Change the direction of the string twice, with two loops over the chair, so the feather moves the opposite way to your hand.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own machine. Score your own hand stroke, then score your machine stroke. Did the machine tickle more? If not, change it and try again.

flow.do: Read the challenge together.
flow.say: Scientists found a small delay can make your own touch tickle. Can we build something like that?
flow.kid: Can you build a machine to tickle yourself?

flow.do: The child builds and changes a machine with string, a ruler and tape.
flow.say: What will make the feather move later than your hand, or in a different direction?
flow.kid: Build it. Try it. Change it.

flow.do: Test fairly and compare scores.
flow.say: Score your hand stroke. Now score your machine stroke. Which was higher?
flow.kid: Score your hand. Score your machine. Which tickled more?
flow.parent: It may or may not tickle more. Either result is useful. Ask the child why they think it worked or didn't.

setup.art: A string looped over the back of a chair, a feather tied to one end near a child's bare foot, and the child pulling the other end down.
setup.caption: 1. Loop a string over a chair and tie on a feather.

setup.art: A feather taped to the end of a long ruler, held by a child at the other end.
setup.caption: 2. Or tape a feather to a ruler.

items.p: In the Tickle Test, you stroked your own foot with a feather, and then someone else stroked it. Whose stroke tickled you more?
items.why: For most people, someone else's stroke tickles more. Your brain predicts your own stroke and turns it down.

items.p: In the Tickle Test, you scored each tickle with four faces, from 0 to 3. Draw the four faces.
items.a: A straight face for 0, a small smile for 1, a big smile for 2 and a laughing face for 3.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the four faces in order, so anyone can see what each score means.

items.p: Will a stroke on your foot tickle less if you do it yourself, or if someone else does it? Why? Say your answer out loud, and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: My own stroke tickles less. My brain knows exactly when and how my own hand will move, so it expects the touch.
items.why: A strong answer makes a guess and gives a reason: the brain predicts its own movements.

items.p: In the tickle test we used the same feather, the same spot and the same number of ___ each time.
items.why: Keeping everything the same except who strokes makes the test fair.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to what it tells us.
pairs: my brain knows my own touch
I hear my voice from the inside
items.why: Each activity showed a different part of knowing yourself: your touch, your voice and your likes.

items.p: Label the picture: the way sound goes through the air, and the way sound goes through the bones of the head.
a: the lines from the mouth to the ear outside are through the air
the lines inside the head are through the bones
items.why: You hear both kinds of sound from your own voice. Other people hear only the sound in the air.
items.art: A side view of a child's head while talking, with wavy lines from the mouth round to the ear, and wavy lines inside the head to the ear.

items.p: Kavya, a girl aged 7, and her father (Appa) talk about the tickle test.

views.says: You can't tickle yourself because you know the touch is coming.
My eyes were shut and I knew my grandmother was going to stroke me, but it still tickled. So knowing is not enough.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right. A grown-up can write your answer.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. Kavya's test shows knowing when is not enough. Appa is partly right: the brain does predict your own touch, very exactly.
items.why: Both views use the idea of knowing. The test shows the brain must predict the exact moment and way, which only works for your own movements.

items.p: Your shadow moves whenever you move. Is your shadow part of your body?
opts: Yes, it is made of the same stuff as your skin
No, it is a patch where your body blocks the light
Yes, because you can feel it
items.why: Your shadow is a dark patch where your body stops light. It is not made of anything from your body.

items.p: You put a sticker on your right cheek. Which one shows you the way your friends see you: the mirror or the photo?
items.why: A photo shows you the way other people see you. A mirror shows your sides swapped.

items.p: When you hum with two fingers on your throat, your throat ___.
items.why: Sound is made by things that vibrate, which means they shake back and forth very fast. You can feel your throat shaking.

items.p: Riya records her voice and says 'That's not me!' Her friend says 'That's just like you.' Who is right?
opts: Both: Riya hears it from the inside, her friend from the outside
items.why: Riya hears her voice through her bones too, so it sounds deeper to her. Her friend hears it only through the air, like the phone.

items.p: A boy strokes his own foot hard, and his sister strokes it gently. He says his own stroke tickled less. What is wrong with his test?
items.a: The strokes were not the same. He should stroke the same way as his sister.
items.why: A strong answer spots that two things changed: who stroked and how hard. A fair test changes only one thing.

items.p: Sort these into touches your brain usually turns down, and touches you notice at once.
items: an ant walking on your arm
items.why: Your brain turns down touches that are always there or that you make yourself. New touches from outside are noticed straight away.

items.p: True or false: newborn babies react the same way to their own hand on their cheek as to someone else's finger.
items.why: False. In a study, newborns turned their head more to someone else's finger than to their own hand.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl aged 8, and her grandmother (Ammamma) talk about flowers that reject their own pollen.

views.says: Many flowers know their own pollen and keep it out. So a flower has a sense of self.
A sense of self means knowing 'this is me'. The flower's pollen check is more like a lock and key.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say what the other person has right. A grown-up can write your answer.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses a fact: the flower tells their own pollen from other pollen. It also says what the other side means.
items.why: Scientists argue about this. Both sides use the same fact, that the flower rejects their own pollen. But they mean different things by 'sense of self'.

items.p: Put the steps of the tickle test in order.
items: stroke your own foot five times
a: stroke your own foot five times
items.why: First guess, then test both ways, then count.

items.p: Draw yourself looking in a mirror with a sticker on your right cheek. Draw where the sticker is on the mirror you.
items.a: In the mirror, the sticker is on the side of the mirror face that is nearest your own right hand. In a photo it is on the other side.
items.why: In a mirror your sides look swapped compared with a photo. A strong drawing shows the sticker on the other side in the photo.

items.p: Why does humming with your fingers in your ears sound louder?
opts: The sound through your bones stays inside your head
items.why: With ears blocked, less sound leaks out, so you hear more of the sound that travels through your bones.

items.p: Name one like that changed since you were three. Why do you think it changed?
items.a: I didn't like idli, but now I do, because I ate it every week.
items.why: A strong answer names a real like and gives a reason, such as trying it often, growing or friends.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Your hand, your foot, your shadow, your nose.
items.why: You can feel your hand, foot and nose being touched. Nobody can touch your shadow and make you feel it.

worksheets.title: Who Else Tells Their Own from Another's? (challenge)

items.p: A male cricket's hearing turns down while he sings. How is that like the tickle test?
items.a: In both, the body turns down a feeling it makes itself, so the cricket isn't deafened and my own stroke doesn't tickle.
items.why: A strong answer says both turn down something they make themselves.

items.p: Two girls, Meenakshi and her friend Divya, talk about the glove hand test, where a glove is stroked while your real hand is hidden.

views.says: The glove felt like my hand. So my brain decides what is me by what I see and feel together.
It didn't work on me at all. So the glove test doesn't show anything.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. What would you test next to find out more? A grown-up can write your answer.
items.a: A strong answer sees that the test worked for one person and not the other, which is a real result. Meenakshi's idea fits her result. Divya is right that it doesn't work for everyone. Next, test more people, with strokes at the same moment and at different moments.
items.why: Scientists found the glove trick works for many people, not all. One person's result is not enough either way.

items.p: Scientists made a robot that touched a person's hand a tiny moment after the person moved a lever. What happened?
items.why: With a small delay, the touch no longer matched what the brain predicted, so it was not turned down as much.

items.p: Draw a machine that could let you tickle yourself. Label the part you move and the part that touches your foot.
items.a: A drawing with labels, for example a string over a chair with a feather on one end.
items.why: A strong design makes the feather move later than the hand, or in a different direction.

items.p: A girl says, 'I know exactly how my friend feels, because I can see her face.' Is she right? Why?
items.a: Not completely. A face gives clues, but only her friend feels it from inside. She should ask.
items.why: A strong answer says others only see clues, and asking is the way to know.

items.p: Label the brain picture: the message to the hand, and the copy the brain keeps.
a: the dotted arrow that stays in the brain
items.why: The brain keeps a copy of each movement message, and uses it to predict what you will feel.
items.art: A child's head and arm, with a solid arrow from the brain to the hand and a dotted arrow curling back inside the brain.

items.p: Match each living being to how they tell their own from another's.
pairs: turns more to someone else's touch
items.why: Each being tells self from other in their own way.

items.p: True or false: if the glove never feels like your hand, you did the test wrong.
items.why: False. The glove trick works for many people but not for everyone. If nothing happens, that is a real result too.

items.p: In the glove hand test, you stroke the glove and your hidden hand at the same moment. Which second try is a fair comparison?
opts: Using a different glove and a different person
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Here only the timing of the strokes changes.

items.p: Put the steps of the glove hand test in order.
items: stroke the glove and the hidden hand at the same moment
hide the real hand behind a book
put the glove where you can see it
a: hide the real hand behind a book
put the glove where you can see it
stroke the glove and the hidden hand at the same moment
items.why: First hide the hand and set up the glove, then stroke, then ask.

videos.check: Found by search: "Why can't you tickle yourself?" by SciShow, 2 min 41 s. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: What is a sense of self?
quiz.why: A sense of self is knowing that your body, likes and feelings are yours.

quiz.p: Why does your own stroke on your foot tickle less?
opts: Your brain predicts it and turns it down
quiz.why: Your brain keeps a copy of your movement and predicts the touch, so it feels weaker.

quiz.p: In a fair tickle test, what should change?
quiz.why: Change only one thing, so you know what made the difference.

quiz.p: Why does your voice sound strange on a phone?
opts: The phone records only the sound in the air
quiz.why: You also hear your voice through your bones. The phone records only the sound in the air.

quiz.p: A boy did not like curd when he was 3. Now he loves it. What does this show?
quiz.why: Many likes change as we grow and try things again.

quiz.p: Many flowers can tell their own pollen from pollen of another plant. What do the flowers do with their own pollen?
quiz.why: Many flowers know their own pollen and stop it from making seeds.

quiz.p: A cricket sings very loudly. What happens to his hearing while he sings?
opts: It turns down for a moment
quiz.why: His hearing turns down while he sings, so his own song does not deafen him.

quiz.p: Who can feel your feelings from the inside?
quiz.why: Others see clues like your face. Only you feel the feeling inside.

quiz.p: When you sit still, you stop feeling your shirt. Why?
opts: Your brain turns down touches that don't change
quiz.why: Your brain turns down touches that are always there, so you can notice new ones.

quiz.p: Which of these would your brain NOT turn down?
opts: A mosquito landing on your arm
quiz.why: Your brain turns down touches that are always there or that you make yourself. A new touch from outside is noticed at once.

applications: Doctors check how newborn babies turn to a touch on the cheek, to see that the baby's body is working well.
Researchers are testing whether the glove hand idea can help people who have lost an arm feel that a new artificial hand is their own.
Singers and radio presenters learn to listen to recordings of themselves, because the recording is how listeners hear them.
Teachers ask children what they feel instead of guessing from their faces.

open_questions.q: Is there one place in the brain where 'me' is?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have not found one 'me' spot. Many think the feeling of 'me' comes from many parts working together. Nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: Why does the glove trick work for some people and not others?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are still studying why some people feel the glove as their own hand, and others don't.

ask_kids: Which of your likes do you think will change by the time you are 10?
If you could hear your voice the way other people hear it, would you like it?
What is one thing about you that nobody else knows?
How do you know your hand is yours?
Which feeling did you have most today?

jokes.j: Why couldn't the girl tickle herself?
jokes.a: Her brain always told on her!

jokes.j: Why did the man record his voice ten times?
jokes.a: He kept hoping the phone would get it right!

jokes.j: What does a mirror say when you wave your right hand?
jokes.a: I'll wave my left, thank you.

jokes.j: Why did the cricket stop listening while he sang?

jokes.a: Follow the leader, every single time.

jokes.j: Why did the boy put his fingers in his ears and hum?
Why did the flower say no to their own pollen?
jokes.a: They wanted to meet someone new!

jokes.j: What did the girl say when she saw her photo?

maths.problem: In a family tickle test, 5 people tried. 4 people scored their own stroke lower than someone else's. 1 person gave both strokes the same score. How many more people scored their own stroke lower than gave both the same score?
maths.explain: 4 take away 1 is 3. Most people in the family found their own stroke tickled less.
maths.context: This is about the tickle test, where each person scored their own stroke and someone else's stroke.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the counts shows how strong the pattern is, not just that it happened once.

maths.problem: In the story Kavya's Two Voices, Kavya's scores for her own stroke were 0 and 1. Her scores for her grandmother Ammachi's stroke were 3 and 3. Add each pair. How much bigger is the total for Ammachi's stroke?
maths.explain: 0 + 1 = 1. 3 + 3 = 6. 6 take away 1 is 5. Ammachi's stroke tickled much more.
maths.context: This is about the tickle test in the story Kavya's Two Voices, where Kavya had two tries of each kind of stroke.
maths.why_maths: Adding two tries together evens out a fluke, so the totals are fairer to compare.

maths.problem: Make a tally of your family's answers to 'Does the recording sound like you?' 6 people said yes and 2 said no. Draw the tally marks.
maths.answer: Yes: a gate of 5 and 1 more. No: 2 marks.
maths.explain: A gate is four lines with one across. 6 is one gate and one line. 2 is two lines.
maths.context: This is about the recording activity, where you asked people if the recording sounds like you.
maths.why_maths: A tally lets you count answers quickly as people give them.

maths.problem: On your then and now sheet, 5 likes were written. 3 of them changed. How many stayed the same? Is that more or less than half?
maths.answer: 2 stayed the same. That is less than half.
maths.explain: 5 take away 3 is 2. Half of 5 is two and a half, so 2 is less than half. Most of the likes changed.
maths.context: This is about the then and now activity, where you compared your likes at 3 with your likes now.
maths.why_maths: Saying more or less than half tells you at once whether most of your likes changed or stayed.

warmup.q: Why does your voice sound different on a phone?
warmup.a: The phone picks up only the sound in the air. You also hear your voice through the bones of your head.

warmup.q: Is your face in a mirror the same way round as your face in a photo?
warmup.a: No. In a mirror your sides look swapped compared with a photo.

warmup.q: What does a flower do with their own pollen?
warmup.a: They stop it from making seeds.

What is it called when you know you are you?

roots.context: We have tested how your body knows its own touch, voice and likes. Now we ask what the tickle test tells us about who we are.

deep_truth.truth: When you stroked your own foot, it hardly tickled. When someone else stroked it the same way, you laughed. Your brain predicts each touch you make. So your body tells your own touch from another's before you think about it.
deep_truth.habit: We think knowing who we are is something we work out by thinking about it. But the tickle test shows the body sorts 'my touch' from 'another's touch' all the time, before any thought.
deep_truth.evidence: In the tickle test, with the same feather, spot and strokes, most people scored their own stroke lower than someone else's.

three.who_am_i: Your brain keeps track of every movement your body makes, so it knows which touches are yours.
three.what_is_life: Many living beings tell their own from another's. A newborn baby turns more to someone else's finger than to their own hand. A flower knows their own pollen. A cricket turns down his hearing for his own song.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of beings who each know their own touch, their own song or their own pollen.

roots.thread: A baby, a flower and a cricket each tell their own from another's, in their own way. You do it with touch: your brain predicts your own touch and turns it down. Telling 'me' from 'not me' starts in the body, before words.

teachings.source: Ramana Maharshi, Nan Yar? (Who am I?), Tiruvannamalai, teachings recorded from about 1902
teachings.teaching: Ramana Maharshi, a teacher from Tamil Nadu, asked people to look for the 'I' that notices everything. He said to keep asking 'Who am I?'
teachings.link: In this unit you asked 'who am I?' with tests: whose touch, whose voice, whose likes. Your body already answers part of it, by knowing its own touch.

teachings.source: The inscription 'Know thyself' at the temple of Apollo at Delphi, as recorded by Plato in Protagoras 343b
teachings.teaching: Ancient Greeks carved the words 'Know yourself' at a famous temple. Many thinkers took it as the first step to wisdom.
teachings.link: Knowing yourself turns out to include surprises: your voice sounds different to others, and your mirror face is the other way round from your photo.

science.text: Your own touch feels weaker because your brain keeps a copy of the message it sends to your muscles, and uses the copy to predict the touch.
Scientists do not agree on whether plants and insects have a sense of self in the way humans do.

other_view.who: David Hume, a Scottish thinker, in A Treatise of Human Nature, Book 1, Part 4, Section 6 (1739)
other_view.view: Hume said that when he looked inside himself, he only ever found a feeling, a thought or a sight, never a 'self' on its own. He thought the self is a bundle of these, always changing. Many brain scientists today also say there is no single 'me' spot in the brain.

practice.title: Touching and Touched
practice.say: Close your eyes. Put your right hand gently on your left arm. Can you feel your hand touching? Can you feel your arm being touched? Breathe in slowly. Breathe out. Now stroke your arm slowly. Which one is you, the hand or the arm?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Put one hand on your other arm. Feel the hand. Feel the arm. Breathe slowly. Which one is you?

ask: If your brain turns down your own touch, how do you know you are touching anything at all?
Your body tells your own touch from another's before you think about it. What else might your body do for you without thinking?
roots.art: A girl with eyes closed, one hand resting on her other arm, sitting on a mat by a window with a hibiscus plant and a cricket on the sill.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time people simply said you can't tickle yourself because you know the touch is coming. In 1971, Lawrence Weiskrantz and his colleagues at Oxford tested it with a tickling machine. People rated being tickled by someone else as more ticklish than tickling themselves. In the late 1990s, Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, a young scientist in London, worked with Daniel Wolpert and Chris Frith to test this idea more exactly. People moved a lever with one hand. A robot then stroked their other palm with soft foam. With no delay, the stroke hardly tickled. When the robot added a delay of a fraction of a second, or moved in a different direction, the same stroke tickled more. The people still knew the touch was coming, because they made it. So knowing was not enough. The brain predicts the exact touch from the movement, and turns down only what matches. Brain scans showed a part at the back of the brain, called the cerebellum, helps make this prediction.
how_we_found_out.who: Lawrence Weiskrantz and colleagues at Oxford, then Sarah-Jayne Blakemore with Daniel Wolpert and Chris Frith in London
how_we_found_out.when: The first tickling machine study was in 1971. The robot studies were in 1998 and 1999.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought you can't tickle yourself only because you know the touch is coming. Blakemore's robot showed that even when people knew, a tiny delay made their own touch tickle again.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist in a lab beside a small robot arm with a piece of soft foam, and a volunteer moving a lever with one hand while the other palm lies under the foam.

playtest: Walked through the tickle test, the glove hand test and the recording, mirror and then-and-now activities as a parent and child in a flat, with only a feather, a rubber glove, a book, a towel, a phone and a mirror. The tickle test now has the child open their eyes before pointing to a face, and the glove test gets a rest between tries and a set distance for the glove, with a note that it may not work for everyone. Me or Not Me now has a clear stack order and an end with no winner, and the cards no longer say a mirror flips left to right. The Me book steps now match its five-day schedule, no step assumes a grandmother or sibling at home, and repeated worksheet and quiz questions were replaced with new ones.
